title: The Rehashing Problem
description: Discover why naive modulo-based hashing breaks when servers are added or removed, setting the stage for consistent hashing.

segments.text: Alright, let's talk about one of the most elegant solutions in distributed systems. But before we see the solution, we need to feel the pain of the problem it solves.
Picture this. You're running a web application, and you've got four database servers to store your data. Server zero, server one, server two, and server three. Each one is humming along nicely.
Now here's the question: when a new piece of data comes in, how do you decide which server stores it? You need a system that's fast, deterministic, and spreads data evenly.
segments.thought_prompt: How would YOU decide which server stores each piece of data?

segments.text: The simplest approach? Modulo hashing. Take the data's ID, divide by the number of servers, and use the remainder. It's elegant in its simplicity. Data ID seven goes to server three, because seven mod four equals three.

Let's see it in action. Data item seven: seven mod four is three, goes to server three. Data item twelve: twelve mod four is zero, goes to server zero. Data item twenty-five: twenty-five mod four is one, goes to server one. Beautiful, right?
This works perfectly. Every piece of data has a clear home. Lookups are instant — just compute the hash, and you know exactly where to go. No searching, no guessing.
But here's where I need you to think. Really think about this.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if server 2 suddenly crashes? Where does its data go now?

segments.text: Server two goes down. Crashed. Gone. Now you have three servers instead of four. And this is where everything falls apart.

With three servers, the formula changes. Seven mod three is one — not three anymore. Data item seven needs to move to a completely different server! Twelve mod three is zero — okay, that one stays. But twenty-five mod three is one — it moved too!

It's not just the crashed server's data that moves. When the modulo changes, approximately seventy-five percent of ALL data needs to be relocated. Three out of every four items end up on a different server. If this is a cache, you just lost seventy-five percent of your cache hits. Instantly.

I've seen this exact scenario bring down production systems. A cache cluster loses one node, seventy-five percent of requests suddenly miss the cache and slam into the database. The database can't handle the load, response times spike, and you've got a cascading failure on your hands at three in the morning.

This is the rehashing problem. And in the next lesson, we'll see how consistent hashing solves it elegantly — moving only a fraction of the data when servers come and go. But the key takeaway right now? Simple solutions that work at small scale can be catastrophic at large scale. That's the recurring theme of distributed systems.
